title: PostgreSQL Generated Column: Virtual vs Stored (PostgreSQL 18)
description: PostgreSQL generated columns explained with real output: virtual vs stored in PostgreSQL 18, indexing, ALTER TABLE, JSONB and the errors you will hit.

reviewNotes: Regular (Sunday) article, not a series part. Tested on PostgreSQL 18.6 (Ubuntu 18.6-1.pgdg24.04+2) from the PGDG repository on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS; followed the PostgreSQL 18 documentation (docs/current pages in sources) plus the 17.0 and 18 release notes. All outputs are real and come from one run in article order on a fresh scratch database 'shop', except the virtual-column expression-index EXPLAIN, which I re-ran after adding the ANALYZE shown in the article (without ANALYZE the planner chose a parallel seq scan). Long psql headers/plan lines were only trimmed of trailing spaces; the filenode values and the 50 MB / 66 MB sizes will differ slightly for readers. SANDBOX CAVEATS: (1) As in earlier runs, postgresql-18 needs liburing2 from archive.ubuntu.com, which is blocked here; I installed a local stub liburing.so.2 package (only io_method=io_uring would use it; the default is worker). The 18 main cluster was created with pg_createcluster because the image already had a 16 cluster. (2) The 'syntax error at or near ")"' for omitting STORED was captured on PostgreSQL 16.15 (the image's distribution package); the callout labels it as PostgreSQL 16. EDITOR CHECKS: (a) 'PostgreSQL 12 to 17 only had STORED' (FAQ): generated columns first appeared in 12; I did not re-read the 12 release notes this run. (b) The numeric(12,2) cast gotcha (common mistake 5) and the 'concat_ws/to_char are not immutable' errors are from my tests, not from the docs text. (c) The statement that the planner guesses selectivity for virtual columns is my inference from 'virtual generated columns never have statistics' (ALTER TABLE page). (d) The pages ranking for this keyword (neon/postgresqltutorial) still say only STORED is supported, which is the gap this article fills. Related links: DBA Part 11 (MVCC, cited in best practices) and the upsert article (both live).

data.text: A PostgreSQL generated column is a column whose value is always calculated from other columns in the same row. You declare it with GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expression), and PostgreSQL fills it in for you. You can never write to it yourself.

PostgreSQL 18 changed how these columns work. There are now two kinds: virtual (calculated when you read the row, no disk space) and stored (calculated when you write the row, saved on disk). Virtual is the new default. Many tutorials still say "PostgreSQL only supports STORED", which was true up to PostgreSQL 17 and is no longer correct.

This guide shows both kinds on a small orders table, with real output from PostgreSQL 18. You will see how to add a generated column to an existing table, why you cannot index a virtual column (and the workaround), how to change or drop the expression, and the error messages you will hit along the way.
What is a generated column?

Think of a generated column as a formula cell in a spreadsheet. You type the quantity and the unit price, and the total cell works itself out. If someone changes the quantity, the total changes too. Nobody can type a different number into the total cell.

The documentation puts it this way: a generated column is for columns what a view is for tables. A virtual generated column is like a view (worked out on every read). A stored generated column is like a materialized view that refreshes itself automatically every time the row is inserted or updated.

content: When the row is inserted or updated
ADD COLUMN on a big table

data.text: The syntax is the same for both. Add the keyword VIRTUAL or STORED at the end, or leave it out to get virtual:

data.code: column_name data_type GENERATED ALWAYS AS ( expression ) [ STORED | VIRTUAL ]
data.caption: Column definition syntax

data.title: Version difference
data.text: Before PostgreSQL 18, the STORED keyword was required. If you leave it out on PostgreSQL 16, you get ERROR: syntax error at or near ")". On PostgreSQL 18 the same statement works and creates a virtual column. If your scripts must run on older versions too, always write STORED explicitly.
Sample setup: an orders table

Connect to a scratch database with psql (for example sudo -u postgres psql -d shop on Ubuntu) and create this table. It has one virtual column (line_total) and one stored column (total_gst, the total including 18% GST).

data.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id     integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer     text          NOT NULL,
    quantity     integer       NOT NULL,
    unit_price   numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    discount_pct numeric(5,2)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    line_total   numeric(12,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS
                   (quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount_pct / 100)),
    total_gst    numeric(12,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS
                   (round(quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount_pct / 100) * 1.18, 2)) STORED
);

INSERT INTO orders (customer, quantity, unit_price, discount_pct) VALUES
  ('Asha',  2,  499.00,  0),
  ('Ravi',  1, 1299.00, 10),
  ('Meena', 5,  120.50,  5);
data.caption: Create the sample table and rows

data.text: Notice that the INSERT lists only the normal columns. You never supply values for line_total or total_gst.
Reading and updating generated columns
Step 1: select the rows

Both columns look like ordinary columns to the query. For Meena the raw result is 572.375, and the numeric(12,2) column type rounds it to 572.38. The declared type of a generated column applies to its result, just as it would for a normal column.
Step 2: check which kind each column is
The catalog table pg_attribute has a column attgenerated: v means virtual, s means stored, and an empty string means a normal column.

data.code:
SELECT attname, attgenerated
  FROM pg_attribute
 WHERE attrelid = 'orders'::regclass
   AND attgenerated <> '';

attname   | attgenerated
------------+--------------
 line_total | v
 total_gst  | s
(2 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: In psql, \d orders also shows the expression in the Default column, with the word stored at the end for stored columns and nothing for virtual ones.
Step 3: update a base column

Both values followed the new quantity. The stored column was recomputed during the UPDATE and written into the new row version. The virtual column was simply computed again when the SELECT read the row.
Step 4: try to write a generated column

data.code:
INSERT INTO orders (customer, quantity, unit_price, line_total)
VALUES ('Kiran', 1, 100, 100);

ERROR:  cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "line_total"
DETAIL:  Column "line_total" is a generated column.
data.caption: Output

data.code: UPDATE orders SET total_gst = 0 WHERE order_id = 2;

ERROR:  column "total_gst" can only be updated to DEFAULT
DETAIL:  Column "total_gst" is a generated column.
data.caption: Output

data.text: The only value you may give a generated column is the keyword DEFAULT. That is handy when a tool or ORM always sends every column in the INSERT:
Virtual vs stored: disk space and table rewrites
How much space does a stored column use?
To see the storage difference, create two identical tables with one million rows. The only difference is VIRTUAL versus STORED on the two generated columns.

data.caption: Compare table sizes

data.code:
relname    | table_size
---------------+------------
 sales_virtual | 50 MB
 sales_stored  | 66 MB
(2 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: In this test the stored version is about a third larger, because the amount and summary values sit in every row on disk. The virtual table holds only the id, quantity and unit price, yet it returns the same values:

data.code: SELECT id, amount, summary FROM sales_virtual ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

data.text: Smaller tables mean fewer pages to read and less to back up. The price is that a virtual column is computed again on every read, so a heavy expression read millions of times costs CPU every time.
Adding a generated column to an existing table

You add a generated column with ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN. The two kinds behave very differently on a big table. The documentation says adding a stored generated column rewrites the entire table and its indexes, while adding a virtual one never requires a rewrite. You can see this with pg_relation_filenode(), which returns the number of the file that holds the table. A rewrite creates a new file, so the number changes.

The virtual column left the file alone, so the ALTER finished almost instantly. The stored column made PostgreSQL write a brand new copy of the table. Your file numbers will differ; what matters is whether the number changes.

data.title: Locking on big tables
data.text: A table rewrite holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole time, so nobody can read or write the table until it finishes. On a large production table, adding a STORED generated column can block your application for minutes. Add a VIRTUAL column instead, or schedule the change in a maintenance window.
Can you index a generated column?
Virtual columns cannot be indexed

data.code: CREATE INDEX sales_virtual_amount_idx ON sales_virtual (amount);
ERROR:  indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported
data.caption: Output

data.text: This is a current limit of PostgreSQL 18. Stored columns are indexed like any other column, and the planner uses the index directly:

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Index Only Scan using sales_stored_amount_idx on sales_stored
         Index Cond: (amount > '9900'::numeric)
(3 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Workaround: an expression index on the same formula

When a query reads a virtual column, PostgreSQL replaces the column with its expression before planning. So an expression index built on exactly the same formula can serve queries on the virtual column. Run ANALYZE after creating it so the planner has statistics for the indexed expression.

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on sales_virtual
         Recheck Cond: (((quantity)::numeric * unit_price) > '9900'::numeric)
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on sales_virtual_amount_expr_idx
               Index Cond: (((quantity)::numeric * unit_price) > '9900'::numeric)
(5 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The query says amount > 9900, but the plan shows (quantity)::numeric * unit_price. That is the virtual column being expanded, and the expression index matches it. If you need a plain index on the column itself, use STORED.
Statistics: another difference
ANALYZE collects statistics for stored generated columns but never for virtual ones. You can check in pg_stats:

data.code:
attname | n_distinct
---------+------------
 amount  |        801
(1 row)

 attname | n_distinct
---------+------------
(0 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Without statistics, the planner guesses how many rows a filter on a virtual column returns. For a column you filter on often, a stored column (or an expression index, which gets its own statistics) gives the planner better estimates.
Generated column from JSONB
A common real use is pulling one field out of a JSONB document into a proper column, so you can index it and query it simply. The ->> operator is built in and immutable, so it is allowed.

data.code:
customer_id | name  |  city
-------------+-------+---------
           1 | Asha  | Pune
           2 | Ravi  | Chennai
           3 | Meena |
(3 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Meena's profile has no city key, so city is NULL. When the JSON changes, the column follows:

data.code:
customer_id |   city
-------------+-----------
           3 | Bengaluru
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: STORED is the right choice here because we want a normal B-tree index on the city column.
Changing or removing the expression
Change the formula with SET EXPRESSION

Say the GST rate on this product changes to 12%. ALTER COLUMN ... SET EXPRESSION AS (added in PostgreSQL 17) replaces the expression. For a stored column, the documentation says existing data is rewritten and the column's statistics are removed, so run ANALYZE afterwards. Virtual columns have no statistics, so ANALYZE is not needed for them.
Every existing row now uses the 12% rate. Because a stored column is rewritten, this also takes a heavy lock on a big table.
Turn a stored generated column into a normal column
DROP EXPRESSION keeps the current values but stops computing them. After this, big_order is an ordinary boolean column you can write to.

data.code: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN big_order DROP EXPRESSION;
ALTER TABLE
data.caption: Output

data.text: The same command on a virtual column fails, because a virtual column has no stored values to keep:

data.code: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN line_total DROP EXPRESSION;

ERROR:  ALTER TABLE / DROP EXPRESSION is not supported for virtual generated columns
DETAIL:  Column "line_total" of relation "orders" is a virtual generated column.
data.caption: Output

data.text: For a virtual column you either drop it (ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN line_total;) or add a new normal column and fill it with an UPDATE.
Common mistakes and the errors they cause
1. Using now() or another non-immutable function

A generation expression may only use immutable functions, meaning functions that always return the same result for the same input. Anything that depends on the clock, settings or other tables is rejected.

data.code: ERROR:  generation expression is not immutable
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: compute values like age in the query (now() - issued_at) or in a view, not in a generated column.
2. Using concat() or concat_ws() for a full name
This one surprises many people. concat_ws is marked stable, not immutable, so it is refused:

data.code: ERROR:  generation expression is not immutable
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: use the || operator on text columns:

data.code:
first_name | last_name |  full_name
------------+-----------+--------------
 Priya      | Sharma    | Priya Sharma
 Arjun      | Nair      | Arjun Nair
(2 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Remember that || returns NULL if either side is NULL. Here both name columns are NOT NULL, so that cannot happen. Formatting a date with to_char() fails for the same reason as concat: it is not immutable.
3. Building one generated column on another

data.code:
ERROR:  cannot use generated column "gst" in column generation expression
LINE 4:   gross   numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS (net + gst)
                                                     ^
DETAIL:  A generated column cannot reference another generated column.
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: repeat the formula, for example GENERATED ALWAYS AS (net * 1.18). Subqueries and references to other tables are also not allowed; a generated column can only see the current row.
4. Calling your own function from a virtual column

data.code:
ERROR:  generation expression uses user-defined function
LINE 3:   gross numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS (add_gst(net))
                                             ^
DETAIL:  Virtual generated columns that make use of user-defined functions are not yet supported.
data.caption: Output

data.text: Virtual columns may only use built-in functions and types. The same function works in a stored column:

Marking a function IMMUTABLE is a promise you make to PostgreSQL. If the function actually reads a table or a setting, PostgreSQL will not stop you, but stored values can become wrong when that data changes. Only mark functions IMMUTABLE when they truly depend on their arguments alone.
5. An expression index that the planner never uses

If the virtual column has a type with a length or scale, like numeric(12,2), PostgreSQL adds a cast to that type when it expands the column. An index on the bare formula then does not match. On the orders table (with sequential scans disabled just for this test, so the planner shows whether it can use the index at all):

data.code:
Seq Scan on orders
   Disabled: true
   Filter: (((((quantity)::numeric * unit_price) * ('1'::numeric - (discount_pct / '100'::numeric))))::numeric(12,2) > '1000'::numeric)
data.caption: Output

data.text: See the ::numeric(12,2) at the end of the filter. Include the same cast in the index and it matches:

data.code:
Index Scan using orders_line_total_cast_idx on orders
   Index Cond: (((((quantity)::numeric * unit_price) * ('1'::numeric - (discount_pct / '100'::numeric))))::numeric(12,2) > '1000'::numeric)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Do not leave enable_seqscan off in real sessions; it is only a testing switch.
Best practices: when to use VIRTUAL and when to use STORED

items.content: Use VIRTUAL for cheap expressions (arithmetic, string joins, JSON field extraction) that you mostly display rather than filter on. You save disk space and can add the column to a huge table without a rewrite.

Use STORED when you need a normal index or a unique constraint on the value, when the expression calls your own IMMUTABLE function, when the column must be logically replicated, or when the expression is expensive and read far more often than written.

Write the keyword explicitly (VIRTUAL or STORED) so the intent is clear to readers and the script behaves the same if it is ever run on an older server (where it fails loudly instead of silently changing kind).
Remember the write cost of STORED. Every UPDATE recomputes and writes it into the new row version. See PostgreSQL DBA Part 11: MVCC for why each UPDATE writes a whole new row.
Prefer a generated column over a trigger for values that come purely from the same row. It is declarative, cannot be overwritten by mistake, and has no PL/pgSQL to maintain.

data.text: Generated columns also carry their own privileges. You can GRANT SELECT (line_total) on a table to a reporting role without granting the underlying price columns. For virtual columns the documentation adds that this is only fully secure if the expression uses leakproof functions.
Frequently asked questions
Is a PostgreSQL generated column virtual or stored by default?
In PostgreSQL 18 the default is VIRTUAL. In PostgreSQL 12 to 17 only STORED existed, and the STORED keyword was mandatory.
Can a generated column reference another table?
No. The expression can only use columns of the current row, with immutable functions and no subqueries. To show values from another table, use a join in a view, or maintain the value with a trigger.
Can I insert a value into a generated column?
No. INSERT and UPDATE may only set it to DEFAULT. Any other value raises "cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column" or "can only be updated to DEFAULT".
How do I convert a generated column into a normal column?
For a stored column, run ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c DROP EXPRESSION;. The values stay and the column becomes writable. This is not supported for virtual columns in PostgreSQL 18.
Does a generated column have a default value?

No. A column cannot be both. If you try DEFAULT 5 GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...), PostgreSQL reports "both default and generation expression specified". A default is applied once at insert and can be overridden; a generated value is recomputed whenever the row changes and can never be overridden.
Summary

items.content: A generated column is computed from other columns of the same row with GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expression)
PostgreSQL 18 adds VIRTUAL generated columns and makes them the default; STORED still exists
VIRTUAL: computed on read, no disk space, no index, no statistics, no table rewrite when added
STORED: computed on write, uses disk, can be indexed, adding one rewrites the table
Only DEFAULT can be written to a generated column
Expressions must be immutable: no now(), concat_ws(), to_char(), subqueries or other generated columns
Virtual columns accept only built-in functions; use STORED for your own IMMUTABLE functions
Index a virtual column's formula with an expression index that matches it exactly, including any type cast
Change the formula with SET EXPRESSION (PostgreSQL 17+) and run ANALYZE after changing a stored column

linkedin.post:
Old tutorials say PostgreSQL only supports STORED generated columns. On PostgreSQL 18 that is wrong.

PostgreSQL 18 added VIRTUAL generated columns and made them the default. Same syntax, very different behaviour:

→ VIRTUAL is computed when you read the row. It takes no disk space. In my test, 1 million rows: 50 MB virtual vs 66 MB stored.
→ Adding a VIRTUAL column with ALTER TABLE needs no table rewrite. Adding a STORED one rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock.
→ You cannot index a virtual column ("indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported"). Use STORED, or an expression index on the exact same formula.
→ The expression must be immutable. now(), concat_ws() and to_char() are all rejected. Use first_name || ' ' || last_name instead of concat_ws.
→ Virtual columns cannot call your own functions yet. Stored ones can.

If your scripts also run on PostgreSQL 17 or older, write STORED explicitly. Leaving it out is a syntax error there.

Which one would you pick for an order total column: virtual or stored?

Full tutorial with examples: link in the first comment.

CREATE TABLE orders (

);
